author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: Three Safe Ways Home
subtitle: Lanternweald — sixth expansion pass
content:
The emergency map had four different colors, and none of them meant what I thought.

"Blue is the accessible ridge path," Pip explained. "Green is the upper canal route when the water is low. Gold is the sheltered walk from the square. Red means closed."

"Then why is the red line drawn all the way to the Threadway?" I asked.

"Because we have to show where people must stop."

I nodded. That made sense, which was precisely why I was suspicious. Too many things had made sense on a map before a person tried to use them.

The working group was meeting in Lanternwell Square. Fen brought tide markers, Tamsin brought inspection sheets, and Neri brought the archive's revised departure rules. Katara was reviewing the clinic's needs; Aang was checking which routes children could use with their caregivers. Toph sat near the stone base of the arch, listening to every cart that crossed the square.

Danse had written the first draft of the emergency checklist.

It was impressively short.

It was also missing a question.

"What if someone doesn't want to leave?" I asked.

He looked at the paper. "If the building is unsafe—"

"What if the building is safe and they prefer to wait there?"

He paused. "Then we tell them their options and respect the choice."

"Can we write that down?"

He added a line.

Edda raised a hand.

"What if I want to leave but can't use the route you've marked?"

Pip turned the map around.

"We have the level ridge path."

"Except last storm that path flooded at the lowest bend."

Tamsin made a note.

"Then we need a third option."

We spent the morning walking the routes rather than arguing about them from the table. The blue path climbed toward the upper ridge and reached the Tideglass Door by a series of level turns. The green path followed the canal, shorter but dependent on tide conditions. The gold route led to the hall, where people could wait safely without crossing into another world.

Three choices did not mean three promises of equal safety.

Each needed conditions and a clear announcement.

At the first junction, Greg joined us carrying a small handbell.

"Thought this might help people hear the route changes," he said.

Toph raised an eyebrow.

"You're going to sing the emergency instructions?"

"Only if everyone agrees the song is catchy."

"Don't."

Greg laughed.

He played a single note and listened to it echo between the buildings. The sound carried well, but Neri pointed out that not everyone could hear it. Pip added a visual signal beside the bell and a written notice at each route entrance.

Maui took the signs from the cart.

"I can hang them."

Pip looked at the map.

"After we check the height."

He held them lower.

"Right."

Iroh arrived with tea and asked whether the waiting hall had enough chairs and hot water. Mara explained the pantry could supply meals for the first day, but not indefinitely. The emergency plan needed a handoff to paid suppliers if the closure lasted longer.

Severus, who had come only to check whether the archive's key procedure was represented correctly, corrected the wording on the private departure form.

"Do not write *may be required to disclose destination*," he said. "That invites unnecessary collection of information."

Neri crossed it out.

People could leave voluntarily. Guides could help. Nobody would be forced through an arch or required to announce which person they were going to see on the other side.

We tested the plan that afternoon.

Edda took the blue route and reported where the gravel had become loose. A parent with two children tried the gold route to the hall and discovered the lantern sign could not be seen around a market stall. A visitor named Beren asked whether they could decline the offered guide without explaining why.

"Yes," Neri said.

Beren declined, then returned to ask for help after realizing the signs weren't yet clear enough.

Nobody treated either choice as a failure.

The test was a mess.

It was a useful mess.

The debrief included one detail I'd almost missed. A visitor had followed the gold route to the shelter, then stopped because the lantern was hung beyond the little ramp and the entrance looked like a service door.

"It was my building," Mara admitted. "I knew which door to use. I forgot a stranger wouldn't."

Pip wrote down the problem. Edda asked the visitor—not the committee—whether they'd describe what had happened. They agreed, on the condition that the report didn't include their name or reason for traveling.

"The sign was visible," the visitor said. "But the path ended at a door I couldn't tell was public."

Maui frowned at the plan.

"Could I paint the door gold?"

"After the owner approves it," Mara said. "And after we choose a color people can distinguish in bad weather."

He nodded, accepting that there was apparently no simple task in Lanternweald that couldn't become a meeting.

We tested a temporary sign from three different approaches, then tried it during a light rain. The first one folded against the wall. The second blocked the handrail. The third worked, once Pip adjusted its height and Mara agreed to keep the landing clear of delivery crates.

The clinic volunteers practiced offering help without insisting that every traveler take their arm. One person chose to wait. Another chose to leave by the ridge path. Nobody demanded proof of fear to justify either decision.

At supper, I pointed out a tiny burn on Maui's finger.

"Lantern hook," he said.

"You should clean it."

"It's almost invisible."

"So is the difference between an invitation and a command until you're the one being given it."

He tilted his head. "That sounded suspiciously wise."

"Don't tell Iroh. He'll charge me tuition."

Maui offered the hand for inspection, wincing theatrically while I washed the scrape. Then he leaned against me, very gently.

"I'd like a quiet evening," he said. "With you. If you don't have other plans."

"I've got a visit tomorrow. Tonight I'm here."

"Good. I will attempt not to schedule an emergency."

We both knew neither of us controlled the weather. The part we could choose was whether to make room for each other when it stopped demanding attention.

After the debrief, Maui found me beside the notice board. He had spent hours carrying supports, not one of which would make a good tale about catching the sun.

"You looked happy," he said.

"I'm exhausted."

"Both can be true."

I smiled.

He pointed toward the map.

"Why three ways? Why not make one perfect route?"

"Because people need different things. And because no route stays perfect in every storm."

He considered that.

"I spent a long time thinking being a hero meant getting everyone to follow me."

"And now?"

"Now I think I should probably ask where they're trying to go."

I kissed his cheek.

He grinned.

A few days later the route signs were installed at their tested heights. The bell signal was paired with lantern markings and written notices. The public instructions listed shelter, voluntary departure, privacy, assistance on request, and the conditions under which each route closed.

At the bottom was a line that had taken the whole committee a ridiculous amount of time to agree upon:

*The safest available option is the one explained clearly enough for the traveler to choose.*

At dusk, I stood beneath the arches and watched people pass.

Some went home to families. Some went to visit friends. Some entered the hall because the wind was cold and they wanted tea.

Nobody had to justify the direction they chose.

Maui stood beside me, holding the final inspection sheet.

"All this work," he said, "and nobody will remember who hung the signs."

"Maybe."

He looked at me.

"That's all right."

Then he took my hand, and we walked toward Tideglass by the gold-lit path, simply because that was where we wanted to go.
